items.followUp: Name the main stages of the cell cycle.

rubric.why: Gives the basic meaning of the cell cycle.
rubric.description: Defines the cell cycle as the sequence of events from one cell division to the next.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition or equivalent description of the cycle of cell growth and division.

rubric.why: Identifies the major parts of the cycle.
rubric.description: Names interphase and the cell-division phase.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both major parts.

modelAnswer: The cell cycle is the sequence of events in which a cell grows and divides, from one division to the next.
It consists of interphase (G₁, S and G₂) and the cell-division phase (mitosis and cytokinesis).

items.followUp: How do cells make ATP during cellular respiration?

rubric.why: Shows that redox reactions transfer electrons or hydrogen between molecules.
rubric.description: Oxidation and reduction occur together as electrons or hydrogen are transferred from one molecule to another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the coupled transfer of electrons or hydrogen in redox reactions.

rubric.why: Connects redox transfer to usable energy in the cell.
rubric.description: Energy released during these reactions is captured to make ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the released energy is used to produce ATP.

modelAnswer: During cellular respiration, oxidation and reduction occur together as electrons or hydrogen are transferred from food molecules to other molecules.
This transfer releases energy, which the cell captures to produce ATP.

items.followUp: What is the role of oxygen in the electron transport chain?

rubric.why: Identifies the electron flow through the chain to oxygen.
rubric.description: The chain passes electrons from NADH and FADH₂ to oxygen, the final electron acceptor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the electron transfer to oxygen.

rubric.why: States an outcome of electron transport that contributes to respiration.
rubric.description: Electron transport helps establish a proton gradient used to make ATP; oxygen accepts electrons and forms water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining ATP production via the proton gradient or for stating that oxygen is reduced to water.

modelAnswer: In the inner mitochondrial membrane, electron carriers pass electrons from NADH and FADH₂ to oxygen, the final electron acceptor.
The energy released helps build a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis; oxygen combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.

items.followUp: What happens to the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction when substrate concentration is increased beyond saturation?

rubric.why: Explains what saturation means for enzyme active sites.
rubric.description: At high substrate concentration, all enzyme active sites become occupied.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the active sites are all occupied or the enzyme is saturated.

rubric.why: States the effect of saturation on reaction rate.
rubric.description: Once saturated, the enzyme works at its maximum rate, so adding more substrate does not increase the rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate reaches a maximum or no longer rises with more substrate.

modelAnswer: As substrate concentration increases, more substrate molecules bind to enzyme active sites until all the active sites are occupied.
The enzyme is then saturated and the reaction rate is at its maximum; adding more substrate does not increase the rate.

items.followUp: Why does an enzyme work best at a particular temperature?

rubric.why: Identifies that enzymes have an optimum pH.
rubric.description: Each enzyme has a particular optimum pH at which its activity is highest.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an enzyme has an optimum pH.

rubric.why: Explains how pH changes enzyme activity.
rubric.description: A pH above or below the optimum changes the enzyme's shape or active site, reducing activity; extreme pH may denature it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking a change in pH to altered active-site shape, lower activity or denaturation.

modelAnswer: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works fastest.
A pH above or below this optimum changes the enzyme's shape, especially its active site, so its activity decreases; extreme pH may denature it.

items.followUp: Give two examples of foods that provide insoluble dietary fibre.

rubric.why: Checks for examples of foods containing soluble dietary fibre.
rubric.description: Names two valid sources of soluble dietary fibre, such as oats, barley, beans, lentils, fruits or vegetables.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each distinct valid source (maximum 2 marks).

modelAnswer: Sources of soluble dietary fibre include oats and barley.
Beans, lentils, fruits and some vegetables are also sources.

items.followUp: Give one example of a plant organ that can act as a sink and later become a source.

rubric.why: Defines a source in terms of food production or export.
rubric.description: A source produces or exports sugars, such as a mature leaf.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of a source.

rubric.why: Defines a sink in terms of food use or storage.
rubric.description: A sink uses or stores sugars, such as a growing region, root or fruit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of a sink.

rubric.why: Explains how a sink can later supply food to other parts of the plant.
rubric.description: A storage sink, such as a tuber or root, becomes a source when stored food is mobilised and exported to growing parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the change from storage/use to food export, with a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A source is a plant part, such as a mature leaf, that produces and exports sugars; a sink is a part that uses or stores sugars, such as a growing region or tuber.
A sink can become a source when stored food is mobilised and exported to other parts of the plant—for example, a tuber supplying food to new growth.

items.followUp: Explain how Biology is related to Physics, Chemistry, Mathematics and Computer Science.

rubric.why: Checks the relationship between Biology and Physics.
rubric.description: Biophysics applies principles of Physics to biological structures and processes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation of biophysics.

rubric.why: Checks the relationship between Biology and Chemistry.
rubric.description: Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and reactions in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation of biochemistry.

rubric.why: Checks the relationship between Biology and Mathematics or statistics.
rubric.description: Biometry uses mathematical and statistical methods to analyse biological data.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation of biometry.

rubric.why: Checks the relationship between Biology and Computer Science.
rubric.description: Bioinformatics uses computers to store and analyse biological information.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation of bioinformatics.

modelAnswer: Biophysics applies the principles of Physics to explain biological structures and processes.
Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and reactions occurring in living organisms.
Biometry uses mathematical and statistical methods to analyse biological data.
Bioinformatics uses computers to store and analyse biological information.
